name: Yongnan Zhuang
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible
sweep_summary: Yongnan Zhuang (yong1275) is not in the catalog. All three title-keyword items Glottolog 5.1 attaches to it (Bögel et al. 2009 LFG09 prosody architecture; O'Connor 2005 LFG05 Serbian clitics, abstract only; Ravignani et al. 2019 animal chorusing) were opened and are computerised-assignment noise: none mentions Zhuang or any Tai-Kadai language and none states where word stress falls in any language. No first-hand statement about word stress in Yongnan Zhuang was read in this search of works with stress in the title. The genuinely relevant descriptions remain unreachable, as in the earlier reading logged in : Zhang Junru et al. 1999 Zhuangyu fangyan yanjiu (print only; has the Yongning/Fusui/Long'an/Shangsi/Qinzhou point phonologies), Luo 2008 'Zhuang' in The Tai-Kadai Languages (Routledge, paywalled), Pan Yanhong 2010 HKU thesis on Qinzhou Zhuang (hub.hku.hk 403 by automated download and direct download, no archived copy at the Internet Archive, CORE 429), Wei Mingying 2017 on the Yongning tone split (CNKI/NCPSSD login).

tone_statements.citation: Liao, Hanbo. 2023. Tonal Behavior as of Areal and Typological Concerns: Centering on the Sinitic and Kam-Tai Languages in Lingnan. Languages 8(2): 148 (44 pp.). Basel: MDPI.
tone_statements.quote: Debao Urban Yang Zhuang only has a two-way split and six tones, but it requires four sets of initials, as its tonal split pattern is 1A-1C/U-1G-2. The other three languages have seemingly more complicated tonal split patterns than Debao Urban Yang Zhuang in terms of three-way split and the tone numbers being seven (Baoxu and Xialeng Zhuang) and nine (Southern Kam), but the required numbers of sets of initials are only three, 1AC-1UG-2 (for both Baoxu Zhuang and Southern Kam), and four, 1A-1CU-1G-2 (Xialeng Zhuang), respectively.
tone_statements.locator: p. 13 of 44, Section 2.2 'Tonal Split Patterns Displayed in a Tone-Box Framework', text following Table 10 'Three-way split pattern in Xialeng Zhuang (Yongnan Zhuang) (Liao 2022, p. 27)'

Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, Australian National University.
tone_statements.quote: The following is intended to provide a preliminary treatment of the initials and tones of Nung An. Like all Tai languages Nung An has syllables with initials, rhymes [...], and a system of six tones. [...] Tones of Nung An. Nung An has six tones on CV syllables and two tones each on CVVC, and CVC, syllables [...] The B tones in Nung An are quite close in pitch trajectory. They are kept distinct not only by pitch but also by voice quality. The tone category 5 is accompanied by tight throat voice at the end of the syllable.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 53-55, Section 2 'Features of the Nùng An language'
tone_statements.n_tones: 6 on CV syllables + 2 on CVVC + 2 on CVC

tone_statements.citation: Nicolson, Beth. 2000. The Nung An language of Vietnam: stepchild or aberrant son? In The Fifth International Symposium on Languages and Linguistics (Pan-Asiatic Linguistics), Ho Chi Minh City, November 2000, vol. 2, 266-295. Ho Chi Minh City: Vietnam National University, HCMC University of Social Sciences and Humanities.
tone_statements.quote: Each reflex from the Nùng An, Cháo, Inh, and Phàn Slình data is followed by a description of its tone contour. ... Another defining characteristic regarding tone is voice quality that accompanies the pitch contour. Edmondson (forthcoming: 6) claims that this is a trait particular to CT. Nùng An clearly has this trait. Tone B1 and B2 in both Quảng Hoà (31□ and 42) and Hà Quảng (42□ and 54□) have a pitch contour that includes either a final glottal (□) or has laryngealization or breathiness (underlining). Final glottal stops also occur with the C2 tone.
tone_statements.locator: first sentence p. 269 below Figure 2; rest p. 274, sec. 2.2 'Voice quality as part of the tone'
tone_statements.summary: Comparative paper: Nùng An tone values (Chao digits) per Gedney box for 2 dialects; B tones glottalized/laryngealized; no inventory or count. Glottal sign prints as a box; 42 underlined. 60+ forms.

sources.citation: Pittayaporn, Pittayawat. 2009. The Phonology of Proto-Tai. PhD dissertation, Cornell University. xix+417 pp.
sources.note: Comparative reconstruction; Yongnan (邕南), Long'an, Fusui, Qinzhou data taken from Zhang et al. 1999, Shangsi from the author's 2009 fieldwork (dialect table p. 322). p. 3: 'All Tai languages are basically monosyllabic and tonal.' 'Stress' appears only in the Proto-Tai prosodic-word/sesquisyllable discussion (p. 42: minor syllable unstressed) and typological asides (Chamic, Latin, Pintupi). No statement about word stress in Yongnan or any modern Zhuang variety.

sources.note: Only the one-page conference abstract exists; it invokes 'tonal behaviors' as subgrouping evidence, presupposing tone, but gives no tone inventory or system and nothing on stress.

tone.quote: Rejecting to the conventional grouping, this paper suggests that YN should be first grouped with NT languages to form a NT-YN sub-branch of which the CT-Southwestern Tai (SWT) sub-branch is a sister, based on evidence from the diachronic hierarchies of linguistic innovations involved in tonal behaviors, initial and vocalic behaviors, as well as exclusive lexical items.
